newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Karadzic fights to retain power in Serb territory.
newsitem.headline: Karadzic fights to retain power in Serb territory.

text.p: Nationalist hardliner Radovan Karadzic pushed through a court ruling designed to undermine the post-war Bosnian Serb president but faces growing international pressure to relinquish his grip on power and face trial for war crimes.

The Bosnian Serb Constitutional Court, under the influence of Karadzic loyalists, said on Friday evening it had struck down a decision by President Biljana Plavsic to dissolve parliament and call general elections in the country's Serb entity.
The court ruling exacerbated a power struggle between Plavsic and Karadzic's allies, who have opposed her attempts to cooperate with Western countries sponsoring the 1995 Bosnia peace treaty.

Analysts had expected the court to rule against Plavsic's move after coming under pressure from government hardliners loyal to Karadzic, the wartime president and now under indictment by the U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia.
Plavsic's aides and Western diplomats had made clear this week they would ignore the ruling because, they said, it lacked legal foundation.

The office of the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, condemned the decision as the product of manipulation and said early elections called by Plavsic should be held as soon as possible.
"The High Representative deplores the ruling of the Republika Srpska (Serb republic) Constitutional Court in what is clearly a decision taken under political pressure," Westendorp's office said.
"New elections under international supervision are the only possible way to resolve this damaging crisis," it added.
Shortly before the ruling was announced, the U.S. State Department accused Karadzic's hardliners of trying to intimidate the court.
State Department spokesman James Rubin said the judges were "under intense political pressure to decide this case. And we are aware of specific acts of intimidation."

With Karadzic allies refusing to participate in early elections, diplomats are concerned the conflict could create two rival authorities, one in Banja Luka run by Plavsic and another in Pale, outside Sarajevo, loyal to the former president.
Balkan analysts said the court decision may have been only a pyrrhic victory for Karadzic, whose once unassailable authority is threatened on several fronts.
During Bosnia's 1992-95 war, Karadzic ruled his conquered territory with impunity, dismissing Western envoys bearing peace proposals and crushing rivals who dared to challenge him.
Now the NATO-led peace force is cracking down on his special police force and his state media network is facing competition from independent press supported by Western governments.

NATO officers announced last week that the Serb special police would have to submit to strict supervision by peacekeeping troops and would no longer be allowed to guard suspected war criminals such as Karadzic.

The commander of the special police, Major General Goran Saric, signed an agreement on Friday pledging that his police would stop providing security for Karadzic, who has refused to stand trial before the U.N. tribunal in The Hague.

NATO would not say if it set a deadline for the special police to withdraw from posts around Karadzic's home and office, but the tougher policy fed speculation that Karadzic might be snatched or spirited to a third country.

U.S. President Bill Clinton discussed Karadzic's status with senior officials on Friday, including the architect of the peace treaty, American envoy Richard Holbrooke, who recently returned from a Balkan tour.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry indicated that major powers were no longer willing to tolerate Karadzic pulling strings in Serb territory.
"He should be concerned that the international community is growing increasingly impatient with the inability of the war crimes tribunal to try the case that he has been indicted for," McCurry said.

Washington said it will deploy extra troops to Bosnia to help provide security for countrywide municipal elections in September. The U.S. contingent, currently just under 8,000 troops, will grow to between 11,000 and 12,000 for several weeks during the mid-September vote.
